summary: A northern Mesopotamian empire that expanded through conquest, provincial administration, tribute and forced population transfers.
capital: Ashur; Kalhu under Ashurnasirpal II; Dur-Sharrukin under Sargon II; Nineveh under Sennacherib and his successors.
rulers: Selected rulers: Ashurnasirpal II, 883–859 BCE; Sennacherib, 704–681 BCE; Ashurbanipal, 668–627 BCE.
economy: Tribute and war booty flowed from conquered regions into Assyria’s capitals.
military: Armies conducted sieges and cavalry campaigns across the Near East; conquered regions supplied tribute and were governed or subordinated to Assyria.
contributions: Monumental palace reliefs, royal archives and Ashurbanipal’s collection preserved major works of Mesopotamian literature and scholarship.
origin: Assyrian kings renewed territorial expansion from northern Mesopotamia during the early first millennium BCE.
decline: Babylonian and Median forces destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE; Assyrian resistance continued afterward.
periodNote: 612 BCE marks Nineveh’s fall, not the instantaneous end of every Assyrian force; sources use later endpoints for the remaining resistance.
